# How to Get Interactive Simulations From Gemini (with Example Prompts)

> **In short:** Gemini can now respond to certain questions with interactive visualizations you can click, rotate, or change parameters on — directly in the chat. You trigger it with the right kind of prompt, and it works on web and mobile with a regular Google account.

You've probably asked an AI something like "explain how a transistor works" and gotten back a wall of text. Read it once, nod, forget it. The Gemini app can now answer some of these questions with something you can actually play with: a molecule you can rotate, a chart with a slider you can drag, or a physics setup where you change a variable and watch what happens. This guide shows you how to ask for that, what kinds of prompts work, and what to do when the first answer is just plain text.

## Before you start

You'll need a Google account — the same one you'd use for Gmail or YouTube. You can use Gemini in a browser at gemini.google.com or in the Gemini mobile app on iOS and Android. The interactive simulations feature is part of the regular Gemini chat, so there's no separate tool to install or enable.

A quick note on terms I'll use below: a **prompt** is just the message you type to the AI. A **visualization** is anything visual — a chart, a diagram, or in this case, something interactive.

## Step 1 — Open Gemini and start a fresh chat

Go to gemini.google.com or open the Gemini app on your phone. Sign in with your Google account if you aren't already. Start a new chat so your question isn't mixed up with old ones.

💬 Example opening prompt:
*"Make me an interactive 3D model of a methane molecule that I can rotate."*

You'll know it worked when the chat is empty, the text box is blinking, and there's no leftover conversation interfering with your new question.

## Step 2 — Ask for something visual and interactive

The trick is to **ask for an interactive result directly**. Don't just ask "what is X?" — ask Gemini to show you X in a way you can manipulate. Words like "interactive", "let me rotate", "let me change", "simulate for me", or "make it clickable" tend to trigger visual responses.

💬 Prompts that tend to work well:
- *"Show me an interactive simulation of a simple pendulum so I can change the length."*
- *"Create a chart where I can adjust the interest rate and see how compound growth changes."*
- *"Give me a 3D model of DNA that I can rotate."*
- *"Build a small simulation of supply and demand where I can drag the sliders."*

You'll know it worked when the response includes something other than paragraphs of text — a chart, a 3D shape, a slider, or buttons you can interact with.

## Step 3 — Try the controls

Once the interactive element appears, actually play with it. On a 3D model, click and drag to rotate. On a chart with sliders, move the slider and watch the numbers update. On a simulation, press play or change a parameter and watch the result shift.

This is the part most people skip — they look at the picture and move on. Spend thirty seconds using the controls. That's where the answer lives.

You'll know it worked when the visualization responds to your input — numbers change, shapes move, lines redraw themselves.

## Step 4 — Ask follow-up questions to dig deeper

Interactive visualizations are usually a starting point, not a final answer. Once you've played with one, ask Gemini to explain what you just saw, or to make a different version with new settings.

💬 Example follow-ups:
- *"Now explain in plain English what happens when I make the pendulum longer."*
- *"Can you make another version where the interest compounds monthly instead of yearly?"*
- *"What does the red line in this chart actually represent?"*

You'll know it worked when Gemini gives you a clear text answer that connects back to what you saw on the screen — the picture and the explanation should fit together.

## Step 5 — Save or share the result

If the simulation is useful, ask Gemini to summarize the key takeaway in plain text you can copy. For 3D models and charts, take a screenshot if you want to keep the image — interactive elements don't always come with a built-in save button.

💬 Example prompt:
*"Summarize the three most important things this chart shows in bullet points I can paste into a note."*

You'll know it worked when you have a clean, copy-pasteable summary sitting next to a visual you'll actually remember.

## Common mistakes

**Asking with words instead of with intent.** "Tell me about photosynthesis" usually gets text. "Show me an interactive diagram of photosynthesis where I can click each part" is much more likely to get a visual response.

**Stopping at the first answer.** If your first response is just text, your prompt was probably too vague. Rephrase it and add the word "interactive", "visualize", or "simulate" — that one word often flips the result.

**Forgetting to actually interact.** The visualization is the point. If you don't click, drag, or change something, you've just traded a wall of text for a static picture — same problem, new format.

**Using it on the wrong kind of topic.** Interactive simulations shine on things that have geometry, motion, or numbers — physics, chemistry, finance, biology. They're less useful for abstract questions like "what is justice?" where there's nothing to draw.

## What this means for you

- **If you're a student**: think of this as a study tool, not a replacement for doing the work. Use it to *understand* a concept after you've read about it once, not instead of reading. Rotate the water molecule. Change the interest rate. Then explain it back to yourself in your own words.
- **If you're a parent helping with homework**: when your kid asks "why?" about a science concept, ask Gemini for an interactive version together. It turns a frustrating explanation into a five-minute experiment you can do at the kitchen table.
- **If you just like learning things**: pick a topic you've always wondered about — how a car engine works, what a black hole looks like, how population growth reshapes a country — and treat Gemini as a sandbox. The prompt is free; the curiosity is the only requirement.

## Wrap-up

Gemini's interactive simulations work best when you ask for them directly. Add words like "show me", "interactive", "let me change", or "simulate" to your prompt, then spend a real minute using the controls. When the visualization answers your question, follow up with a plain-text summary so you actually remember what you learned.

Try this tonight: open Gemini and ask for an interactive simulation of something you learned about once but never really understood — a pendulum, a molecule, mortgage interest, whatever. Play with it for two minutes. That's the whole trick.
